# Volume 5 — CHAPTER II. SHEER GOSSIP

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“Where are the other children?” inquired Miss Winifred, once the initial welcomes—warm from her, ecstatic from Nell, and stately from Tabitha—had concluded.
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0000 }

“Harcourt has gone to bed, while Kit, Edmund, and the twins have gone down to Fern Hollow, which they cherish so much,” Nell stated. “You are aware that they only returned this afternoon, and as soon as supper ended, they hurried off to the valley without delay. To them, it is the most adored place in the world. In their hearts, not even the maple grove can compete with it.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0001 }

“I worry that they are overly fond of it,” Tabitha remarked with a sullen expression. “Young Kit mentioned on one occasion that he preferred going to Fern Hollow over heaven upon his death, which was an inappropriate comment.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0002 }

“I guess they enjoyed themselves immensely in Brierley?” Miss Winifred remarked.
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0003 }

“Immense. Thirza certainly spoils them to an awful degree. Kit, especially, is incapable of doing wrong as far as she is concerned.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0004 }

“Miss Abernethy must be an old woman at this point,” remarked Miss Winifred, retrieving her knitting in order to keep pace with Tabitha. It was Miss Winifred’s belief that a woman with busy hands maintained an upper hand compared to one whose hands remained idle.
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0005 }

“Thirza has reached the age of eighty-five,” sighing, Nell stated. “Snow-white is the color of her hair. Yet, peculiarly, her vision is superior to what it used to be at sixty.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0006 }

“Oh, my sweet, it truly pleases me that everyone has returned. My solitude was terrible. However, life in the Glen was far from boring, you can trust that. Regarding affairs of the church, a spring this thrilling has never occurred during my life. My dear Nell, a pastor has finally been secured by us.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0007 }

“The Reverend John Knox Ashdown, Mrs. Dr. dear,” said Tabitha, who was determined that Miss Winifred would not recount the entirety of the news.
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0008 }

“Is he nice?” Nell inquired with interest.
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0009 }

A sigh came from Miss Winifred, while a groan was uttered by Tabitha.
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0010 }

“Yes, he’s pleasant enough if that were the only thing,” remarked the first speaker. “He is extremely pleasant—and extremely learned—and extremely spiritual. But, oh Nell dearie, he lacks common sense!
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0011 }

“What name did you give him, in that case?”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0012 }

“Well, without a doubt, he is the finest preacher our Glen St. Agnes church has ever possessed,” declared Miss Winifred, shifting her approach slightly. “I imagine his failure to secure a town call stems from his being so dreamy and preoccupied. Take my word for it, his trial sermon was truly extraordinary. Everyone lost their minds over it—and his appearance.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0013 }

“He possesses great attractiveness, Mrs. Dr. dear, and after taking everything into account, I truly enjoy observing a handsome man standing in the pulpit,” interrupted Tabitha, believing she ought to make her presence felt once more.
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0014 }

“Furthermore,” Miss Winifred remarked, “we wanted to be settled soon. Also, Mr. Ashdown was the initial applicant about whom everyone was of one mind. Everyone else faced an objection from someone. Calling Mr. Folsom was mentioned as a possibility. He preached well, too, yet for some reason his look didn't appeal to folks. His complexion was too dark, and his hair was too sleek.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0015 }

“Mrs. Dr. dear, he truly resembled nothing so much as a huge black tomcat,” Tabitha declared. “Every Sunday, I simply couldn’t tolerate a person like that preaching.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0016 }

“Then Mr. Rogers arrived and he resembled a chip in porridge—doing neither harm nor good,” Miss Winifred continued. “However, had he preached like Peter and Cedric it would have availed him nothing, since that was the day old Caleb Ramsay’s sheep wandered into church and uttered a loud ‘ba-a-a’ precisely as he declared his text. Everyone laughed, and poor Rogers stood no chance following that. Some believed we should call Mr. Stewart, as he was so well educated. He had the ability to read the New Testament in five languages.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0017 }

“However, I am doubtful that this gave him any greater certainty than anyone else of reaching heaven,” Tabitha cut in.
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0018 }

“The majority of us were displeased with how he delivered it,” Miss Winifred stated, paying no attention to Tabitha. “It was as if he spoke using grunts, in a manner of speaking. Furthermore, Mr. Arnett possessed no ability to preach whatsoever. On top of that, he selected nearly the most terrible text for candidating that exists within the Bible—‘Curse ye Meroz.’”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0019 }

“Each time an idea eluded him, he used to hit the Bible and scream with immense bitterness, ‘Curse ye Meroz.’ That day, poor Meroz was cursed completely, no matter who he might have been, Mrs. Dr. dear,” Tabitha said.
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0020 }

“A minister who is candidating must exercise extreme caution regarding his choice of text,” Miss Winifred remarked gravely. “In my opinion, Mr. Pierson would have received the call had his selection of a text been otherwise. However, his fate was sealed the moment he declared ‘I will lift my eyes to the hills’. Everyone smiled, because everybody was aware that those two Hill sisters from Harbour Head had been pursuing every sole minister visiting the Glen over the past fifteen years. Furthermore, the family of Mr. Newman was simply too big.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0021 }

“He resided alongside my brother-in-law, James Clow,” Tabitha remarked. “‘What is the number of children you have?’ I inquired of him. ‘Nine boys, plus a sister corresponding to every one of them,’ he answered. ‘Eighteen!’ I exclaimed. ‘My goodness, such a large family!’ And following that, he chuckled repeatedly. However, I remain unaware of the reason, Mrs. Dr. dear, and I feel sure that eighteen children would prove excessive for any manse.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0022 }

“He possessed merely ten children, Tabitha,” Miss Winifred clarified, exhibiting a scornful endurance. “And ten well-behaved children would not cause much more damage to the manse and congregation than the four who reside there at present. Although I would not claim, Nell dearie, that they are that terrible, either. They appeal to me—they appeal to everyone. One cannot avoid liking them. They would turn out to be truly pleasant little beings if somebody were present to manage their conduct and instruct them in what is appropriate and correct. As an example, the instructor at school claims they are exemplary children. At home, however, they are completely untamed.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0023 }

“What about Mrs. Ashdown?” Nell inquired.
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0024 }

“Mrs. Ashdown does not exist. The problem lies right there. A widower is what Mr. Ashdown is. Four years have passed since his wife passed away. Had that been known to us, I do not believe we would have extended an invitation to him, because a widower causes even more difficulty in a congregation than a bachelor. However, people heard him mention his children, so every one of us assumed a mother existed as well. Yet upon their arrival, no one was present except old Aunt Martha, which is what they name her. I think she is a cousin to the mother of Mr. Ashdown, who brought her into his home so she would not end up in the poorhouse. Her age is seventy-five, and she is nearly blind, extremely hard of hearing, and quite ill-tempered.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0025 }

“And an exceedingly bad cook, Mrs. Dr. dear.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0026 }

“Regarding a manse, she is the absolute poorest choice of manager,” Miss Winifred declared with bitterness. “Because he claims it would injure Aunt Martha’s feelings, Mr. Ashdown refuses to hire a different housekeeper. My dear Nell, you must trust me that the manse’s condition is utterly dreadful. A heavy layer of dust covers everything, and not a single item can ever be found where it belongs. Yet, prior to their arrival, we had applied such lovely new paint and wallpaper throughout the entire place.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0027 }

“You mention there are four children?” inquired Nell, whose heart was already starting to nurture them.
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0028 }

“Indeed. They ascend precisely in the manner of stairway steps. Gerald is the eldest. He has reached twelve years of age and people refer to him as Tobias. He is a bright lad. Grace has reached eleven. She proves to be an outright tomboy, though I have to admit she remains as lovely as a image.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0029 }

“She has the appearance of an angel, yet she is a total terror when it comes to mischief, Mrs. Dr. dear,” Tabitha stated with gravity. “One evening last week I happened to be at the manse, and Mrs. James Millison was present as well. She had carried up a dozen eggs and a small pail of milk to them—an extremely small pail, Mrs. Dr. dear. Grace accepted the items and dashed right down to the cellar with them. Close to the foot of the steps her toe caught, causing her to tumble down the remaining distance, along with the milk, the eggs, and everything else. You can picture the outcome, Mrs. Dr. dear. Nevertheless, that girl came back up in laughter. ‘I don’t know whether I’m myself or a custard pie,’ she said. And Mrs. James Millison became extremely furious. She declared that she would not bring a single other item to the manse if it was going to be thrown away and ruined in such a manner.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0030 }

“Maria Millison never harmed herself carrying items to the manse,” Miss Winifred sniffed. “She merely brought them that evening to justify her inquisitiveness. Yet poor Grace continually finds herself in trouble. She displays such carelessness and impulsiveness.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0031 }

“I am just the same, and I shall certainly take a liking to your Grace,” Nell declared with conviction.
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0032 }

“She possesses plenty of spirit—and I truly am fond of spirit, Mrs. Dr. dear,” acknowledged Tabitha.
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0033 }

“She has a certain charm,” Miss Winifred admitted. “Whenever you come across her, she is laughing, and in some way you are always moved to laugh as well. Even during church services, she fails to remain solemn. Ida, who is ten, is an endearing little girl—lacking beauty, yet endearing. Then there is nine-year-old Thomas Carlyle. Going by the name of Rupert, he possesses an absolute obsession with gathering toads, bugs, and frogs to carry inside the home.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0034 }

“I guess he was to blame for the deceased rat that was sitting upon a chair in the parlour during the afternoon Mrs. Hollis visited. It startled her,” stated Tabitha, “and I am not surprised, because manse parlours are not locations for deceased rats. Certainly it might have been the cat that deposited it there. He is as filled with the old Nick as he could possibly be packed, Mrs. Dr. dear. A manse cat ought to at minimum appear dignified, in my view, regardless of what he actually is. However, I have never beheld such a dissolute-appearing creature. Furthermore, he paces across the ridgepole of the manse nearly every night when the sun sets, Mrs. Dr. dear, and swishes his tail, and that is not appropriate.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0035 }

“Their terrible attire is the hardest part,” Miss Winifred sighed. “They have gone to school without shoes ever since the snow melted. You are aware, Nell dearie, that manse children should not behave that way—particularly with the Methodist minister’s little girl constantly wearing those lovely buttoned boots. I also truly wish that the old Methodist graveyard was not their playground.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0036 }

“When it is directly adjacent to the manse, the appeal is strong,” Nell remarked. “Playing in graveyards has always struck me as something that would be wonderful.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0037 }

“Oh, no, you did not, Mrs. Dr. dear,” uttered loyal Tabitha, who was resolved to defend Nell from her own actions. “You possess an excess of sound judgment and propriety.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0038 }

“For what reason did they build that manse next to the graveyard to begin with?” Nell inquired. “Because their lawn is so tiny, they have nowhere else to play besides in the graveyard.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0039 }

“It was an error,” confessed Miss Winifred. “However, they obtained the whole thing at a low price. Furthermore, no other kids from the manse ever considered using that area for recreation. Mr. Ashdown ought to forbid it. Nevertheless, whenever he is present, his face is constantly hidden behind a book. He engages in endless reading, or paces around his study lost in a fantasy. Up until now he has remembered to attend church on Sundays, yet he failed to remember the prayer-meeting on two occasions, requiring one of the elders to travel to the manse to prompt him. Additionally, Fanny Cooper’s wedding slipped his mind. They called him using the ‘phone, whereupon he hurried directly over in his current state, wearing nothing different, carpet slippers included. A person would not care if the Methodists refrained from laughing so much over the matter. Still, a single consolation exists—no one can fault his sermons. Take my word for it, he becomes alert once he stands in the pulpit. Meanwhile, the Methodist minister is completely unable to preach—or so I am informed. I have avoided listening to him, I am glad to say.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0040 }

Although her contempt for men had softened slightly after she wed, Miss Winifred maintained a completely uncharitable disdain for Methodists. A sly smile crossed Tabitha's face.
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0041 }

“It is being reported, Mrs. Ambrose Kerr, that the Methodists and Presbyterians are considering a union,” she said.
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0042 }

“Indeed, my only desire is to be buried in the ground should such a thing ever occur,” replied Miss Winifred. “There will be no dealings or business between the Methodists and me, and Mr. Ashdown ought to realize that staying away from them would be wise for him as well. In my opinion, his friendliness with them goes much too far. To prove my point, attending the silver-wedding feast at the Jacob Drews’ led him straight into a troublesome situation.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0043 }

“What was that?”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0044 }

“Mrs. Drew requested that he carve the roast goose—because Jacob Drew was neither willing nor able to carve. Anyhow, Mr. Ashdown took on the task, and while doing so he struck it right off the platter straight into the lap of Mrs. Coyle, who happened to be seated beside him. Then he simply remarked in a dreamy way, ‘Mrs. Coyle, will you kindly return me that goose?’ Mrs. Coyle ‘returned’ it, as submissive as Moses, though she surely was enraged, since she was wearing her new silk dress. To make matters worse, she was a Methodist.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0045 }

“However, in my opinion, that surpasses her being a Presbyterian,” Tabitha chimed in. “Had she belonged to the Presbyterians, she would, in all probability, have departed from the church, and losing our members is something we cannot afford. Furthermore, Mrs. Coyle is unpopular within her own congregation on account of putting on such grand airs, meaning the Methodists will likely feel somewhat satisfied that Mr. Ashdown ruined her dress.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0046 }

“The point is, he turned himself into a laughingstock, and I, for my part, am not fond of seeing my minister turned into a laughingstock before the Methodists,” Miss Winifred stated rigidly. “Had he possessed a wife, it would never have occurred.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0047 }

“Even if he possessed twelve wives, I fail to understand how that could have stopped Mrs. Drew from consuming her tough old gander for the marriage banquet,” Tabitha asserted stubbornly.
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0048 }

“That was done by her husband, so they say,” Miss Winifred said. “A domineering, stingy, conceited creature is Jacob Drew.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0049 }

“And folks do claim he and his wife hate each other—which doesn't strike me as the right manner for a wedded couple to behave. Though, naturally, I lack any experience in that area,” Tabitha said, tossing her head. “And I don't attribute every fault to the men. Mrs. Drew possesses plenty of meanness herself. People say the sole item she was ever seen to give for free was a butter crock crafted from cream containing a fallen rat. She donated it to a church gathering. The rat remained undiscovered by anyone until later.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0050 }

“Luckily, every individual the Ashdowns have angered up to this point is a Methodist,” Miss Winifred said. “That Tobias attended the Methodist prayer-meeting a single evening approximately two weeks back and took a seat next to aged William Marsh, who stood up in his customary way and bore witness accompanied by terrible groans. ‘Do you feel any better now?’ Tobias murmured softly once William was seated again. Unfortunate Tobias intended to show empathy, yet Mr. Marsh believed he was being rude and is enraged with him. Naturally, Tobias ought not to have been at a Methodist prayer-meeting whatsoever. Nevertheless, they venture wherever they please.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0051 }

“I hope Mrs. Hector Twiss of the Harbour Head will not be offended by them,” said Tabitha. “It is my understanding that she is quite a touchy woman, though she has great wealth and contributes the highest amount toward the salary. According to what I have heard, she claims the Ashdowns are the most poorly raised children she has ever encountered.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0052 }

“All that you utter persuades me increasingly that the Ashdowns pertain to the lineage that is acquainted with Joseph,” declared Mistress Nell with firmness.
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0053 }

“Ultimately, they actually do,” Miss Winifred conceded. “And that makes up for everything. Regardless, we have them in our care now and we simply have to manage as well as possible for them and defend them against the Methodists. Well, I imagine I ought to be heading down harbour. Ambrose will be back home shortly—he traveled over-harbour to-day—and expecting his supper, as men do. I regret that I haven’t met the rest of the children. And where might the doctor be?”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0054 }

“Over at the Harbour Head. It was merely three days ago that we returned, yet throughout this period he has passed no more than three hours sleeping in his own bed and consumed a total of two meals at home.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0055 }

“Indeed, anyone who has been ill over the past six weeks has been anticipating his return—and I cannot fault them. When the doctor from over the harbour wed the undertaker’s daughter in Kettlebridge, folks grew distrustful of him. The appearance of it was bad. You and the doctor ought to visit us shortly and share everything about your journey. I imagine your time was wonderful.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0056 }

“We had,” concurred Nell. “Years of dreams were fulfilled by it. Very lovely and very wonderful is the old world. However, we have returned extremely satisfied with our own country. Miss Winifred, Canada is the world’s finest country.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0057 }

“That was never in question,” Miss Winifred remarked with a sense of self-satisfaction.
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0058 }

“And ancient P.E.I. is the most charming province within it, with Seven Gulls being the most charming location in P.E.I.,” chuckled Nell, gazing with deep affection across the sunset brilliance of the valley, the port, and the gulf. She gestured toward the scene. “I observed nothing that surpassed the beauty of that while in Europe, Miss Winifred. Is it necessary for you to depart? The youngsters will regret not seeing you.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0059 }

“They need to visit me before long. Let them know that there are always doughnuts in the jar.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0060 }

“Oh, during the evening meal they discussed making a raid on your place. Their departure will be shortly; however, returning to their studies requires their attention at present. Furthermore, the twins intend to begin studying music.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0061 }

“I hope it wasn't from the Methodist minister’s wife?” Miss Winifred asked with concern.
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0062 }

“No—from Clementine Ainslie. I went up yesterday evening so that she and I could arrange it. She is such a pretty girl!”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0063 }

“Clementine manages effectively. She is no longer as youthful as she used to be.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0064 }

“She struck me as quite delightful. As you are aware, I have never actually known her well. The place where they live is so remote, and I have rarely spotted her anywhere besides at church.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0065 }

“Clementine Ainslie has always been liked by people, even if she isn't understood by them,” Miss Winifred remarked, entirely unaware that her words were a great compliment to the charm of Clementine. “In a manner of speaking, Harriet has constantly suppressed her. She has dominated her, but she has nevertheless spoiled her in various respects. You are aware that Clementine was engaged at one time—to young Martin Crawford. The Magdalens was where his ship was wrecked, resulting in the drowning of the whole crew. Clementine was merely a child—no more than seventeen. Afterwards, though, she was never quite the same. Ever since the death of their mother, Harriet and she have remained very much at home. They do not reach their own church at Kettlebridge very frequently, and it is my understanding that Harriet dissents from attending a Presbyterian church with any frequency. I will grant her this much, she never sets foot in the Methodist one. Strong Episcopalians have always made up that family of Ainslies. Harriet and Clementine possess a fair amount of wealth. Music lessons do not actually have to be given by Clementine. Her doing so is simply because it pleases her. You know, Lorna is a distant relative of theirs. Will the Treleavens be visiting the harbour during this summer?”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0066 }

“No. Japan is where they are traveling, and their absence will likely last a year. The background for Adrian’s new novel needs to be Japanese. Since the time we departed from the dear old House of Dreams, this coming summer marks the initial one in which it will have no occupants.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0067 }

“Adrian Treleaven ought to discover plenty to author in Canada rather than pulling his wife and his blameless offspring away to a pagan land such as Japan,” complained Miss Winifred. “The Life Book was his finest piece of writing, and he collected the information for it right here in Seven Gulls.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0068 }

“He received the majority of that from Captain Saul, as you are aware. Moreover, his collection was gathered from every corner of the globe. Nevertheless, I consider all of Adrian’s books to be charming.”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0069 }

“Oh, regarding their extent, they are decent enough. It is my rule to peruse each one he produces, even if I have constantly maintained, my dear Nell, that perusing fiction represents an ungodly misuse of hours. Rest assured, I am going to compose a letter informing him about my view on this Japanese affair. Is it his wish for Damaris and Julian to be turned into heathens?”
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0070 }

Following that impossible riddle, Miss Winifred left. Tessa was placed in bed by Tabitha, while Nell remained on the steps of the veranda beneath the young stars, indulging in her persistent fantasies and discovering once more for the hundredth joyful instance the magnificent brilliance and luster of a moonrise over Seven Gulls Harbour.
{: #nw-v05-c02-p0071 }
